appraisal_events.evidence: Swann jokes that the three of them together look like a 'réunion de syndicat,' not noticing Général de Beauserfeuil standing behind him and overhearing; the general 'fronça involontairement les sourcils,' and the narrator states outright that Swann's Jewish humor was 'moins fine que les plaisanteries de l'homme du monde.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's joke misfires: the narrator directly ranks it as inferior wit, and it produces an unintended, faintly hostile reaction from a general who overhears it unnoticed.

appraisal_events.evidence: Victurnien, who 'n'avait jamais lu une ligne' of Balzac but had just had a teacher point out the coincidence of his name with d'Esgrignon's, passes this off as knowledge; Charlus, 'extasié devant tant de science,' praises him as a rare 'jeune homme instruit... chez un des nôtres,' compares him to a Polignac and a Montesquiou, praises the family's art-collecting lineage, and invites him to see his own Balzac collection — flattery the narrator says was calculated to 'enivrer la marquise,' who is 'ravie de voir son fils briller.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus's effusive, rhetorically elaborate praise elevates Victurnien within the aristocratic in-group and flatters his mother by association, though the narrator makes clear the erudition it rewards is entirely feigned.

status_effects.explanation: His joke fails to land as wit and instead produces visible unease in an overhearing listener, marked by the narrator as coarser humor than a society man's.
The general's involuntary frown is a witnessed, if subtle, register of social friction around Swann in mixed company, given the underlying political and ethnic tensions of the moment.
He is praised as learned and 'shines' before Charlus and his delighted mother, even though this praise rests on a misunderstanding the reader is shown but the characters are not.
Charlus explicitly welcomes him into his own aristocratic 'us' ('chez un des nôtres'), a boundary statement of belonging to the true nobility of intellect and heart as Charlus defines it.

Charlus's comparison of her son to a Polignac and a Montesquiou, and his praise of her family's art-collecting lineage, is explicitly framed by the narrator as calculated to flatter and elevate her standing.

ambiguities: Victurnien's apparent erudition about Balzac is fabricated (he has never read the novel), so Charlus's elevation of him rests on a misunderstanding the narrator discloses but the in-scene characters do not share.
